10036498:
Claire Perry Owls Head LD 937
Claire Perry LD 937 SUPPORT
This bill has been badly needed for years and I am encouraged to see that Mr. Mason is its sponsor. Thank you so much.
Baiting carnivores is a contentious issue at best.For many, it is hard to imagine it as hunting. With bears, it is the most humane method available, and enables the shooter to differentiate between a boar or a sow with cubs. I am not opposed.
I have always been opposed to the state-wide baiting of coyotes for several reasons. I do not support the random killing of them for sport, or the misguided notion that one is "saving a deer" in doing so. In the lower third of the state, we could use stable coyote families to help with all the problems of being over-run with deer brings...from tick infestations to garden and crop devastation, to over-grazing of the ecosystems in general.
Worse, are the dead farm animals used as bait. What we do not need to be doing, is enticing a coyote with dead chickens, sheep, or cow parts. The reason is obvious. Or it should be!
Now, I understand this bill does not address all of those issues. And that's okay. If I am right, it will limit the time baiting is permitted, which helps not to have rotting animal carcass' in our woods or on public lands during the warmer/hotter months. It will help stop the putting of bait piles on our lakes in order to pick off a whole family by shooting them or worse, running them down with a snowmobile. It helps raise the status of our coyotes from vermin to a recognized and valuable part of our ecosystems. And no. I don't "love" coyotes. They are a wild predator...just like our bear and bobcat. And just like our bear and bobcat, they deserve to be recognized for the good they bring and to be managed FAR better than what is currently being allowed.
Now, if I am wrong on what this bill is about...so be it. What I said needs to be heard for as many times as it takes to do better by our coyotes. They are not beautiful furry angels...but neither are they the devil.
So thank you for what I HOPE this bill is saying: A permit needed to bait them, specific areas for baiting and a limited season. And if not...thank you for reading my testimony.
Respectfully submitted, Claire Perry

10045682:
Testimony Neither for Nor Against L.D. 937-An Act to Establish a Permit to Hunt Coyote Over Bait
John M. Glowa, Sr. On behalf of The Maine Wolf Coalition, Inc. South China, Maine April 23, 2025
There are no coyotes in Maine. For this reason, this bill is meaningless. I have brought this issue to this committee's attention several times during this legislative session and the committee has failed to consider it.
Maine has coyote/wolf hybrids. All so-called "coyotes" in Maine are coyote/wolf hybrids or wolves. There is no definition of "coyote" in Maine rule or statute.
To my knowledge, there is no prohibition to hunt "coyotes" over bait. Therefore, the reason for this legislation is not known.
For the bill to have any legal meaning, it should be amended to include a science-based definition of "coyote". It should also be amended to require that all canids killed be tagged and brought to the department. Because it is impossible to determine if an animal is a wolf simply by looking at it, the department should be required to have a DNA analysis of every animal meeting certain minimum criterion to include wolf pups.
10045943:
SUSANNA RICHER Portland LD 937
Senator Baldacci, Representative Roberts, and distinguished members of the Committee,
Thank you for considering my comments regarding LD 937, An Act to Establish a Permit to Hunt Coyote over Bait.
While I'm not certain of the motivation behind this bill id, I support any effort to regulate, reduce and track the currently unrestricted and wasteful slaughter of coyote in Maine.
The use of bait to trap and kill animals it's not only unnecessary and inhumane, but dangerous as it trains a coyote that's eating its natural diet of rodents and sick or weak animals, to feed off food that's provided by humans instead.
Additionally, baiting often attracts, injures and sometimes kills unintended wildlife and companion animal species.
Bait piles are often made-up of carrion containing lead ammunition fragments that poison birds of prey such as eagles and the other animals who feed off the bait. The lead tainted bait piles also contaminate our water and soil which results in toxic lead in our plants and in animals that ingest them.
I know many of us would be grateful for any small step forward in the regulation of coyote "hunting" and reduction of wanton waste in our state.
Susanna Richer Portland
